title: Respond to a lawsuit
summary: Being served starts a real deadline. In federal court the answer is due 21 days after service (FRCP 12(a)(1)(A)(i), rule card us-fed.frcp-answer-deadline); state courts set their own, and your summons states yours. In the first week: record how you were served, calendar the deadline, issue a litigation hold (destroying evidence after that is sanctionable), notify any insurer that might owe you a defense, and engage litigation counsel. The response itself, answer, motion, or negotiate, is your lawyer's craft, filed under FRCP 11's signature rule. Educational guidance, not legal advice. The deadline math has exceptions (waived service, the United States as a party); verify with counsel against the rule.

parts.title: Record exactly when and how you were served — the answer clock starts at service
Calendar the answer deadline: 21 days in federal court (FRCP 12(a)(1)(A)(i)); state courts differ — the summons states yours
Issue the litigation hold: preserve documents, chat, email — spoliation is sanctionable
Notify your insurers — D&O, E&O, or CGL may owe you a defense
Decide the response with counsel: answer, motion, or negotiate
Counsel files the response before the deadline (every pleading is signed — FRCP 11)
Wait for the next docket event

metadata.trigger: You've been served: a process server hands you a summons and complaint naming the company.
metadata.supportReason: Litigation strategy, the insurer conversations, and the signed, filed pleadings are counsel work under court rules. An agent can stand up the litigation hold across your systems; it cannot answer a complaint.

geoNotes.summary: Served with a claim form, you acknowledge service and file a defence on the CPR clock — 14 days from the particulars of claim, 28 with an acknowledgment of service; money claims respond online, and silence ends in default judgment.

geoNotes.summary: A served Klage comes with the court's own stated deadlines — typically two weeks to declare the intent to defend (Verteidigungsanzeige) and a further period for the Klageerwiderung; before the Landgericht a lawyer is mandatory (Anwaltszwang), and a missed response risks a Versäumnisurteil.

An assignation names the court and the clock; before the tribunal judiciaire you generally must appoint an avocat (constitution d'avocat) within the summons's stated window — the document itself states your deadline, and default judgment follows silence.

A summons under the CPC sets the date to appear and file the written statement — 30 days, extendable to 90 (and a hard 120-day cap in commercial suits under the Commercial Courts Act); the e-Courts services track the case number end to end.

A served citação starts the clock: the contestação (defence) is typically due within 30 days in ordinary civil proceedings, filed by counsel through the courts' electronic system — the justice portal is the entry point.

Civil procedure is provincial: the summons states your deadline (Ontario gives 20 days from service in-province for a statement of defence) — retain provincial counsel immediately and preserve documents from day one.
